gates.why:
Five tests in one package, 24.5 s together on the reference solution and 24.5 s on the untouched step-7 tree -- the cost is the settle windows, which are the same whether an assertion passes or fails. Three of them are graded here and two are controls in the regression family.

The first counts: six servers started and stopped in turn, against a tolerance of two goroutines. Measured, one start leaks exactly one goroutine on both starting trees -- the loop that takes tasks off a service's queue, which nothing closes -- so six cycles leak six, three times the tolerance. The tolerance is there because the runtime keeps goroutines of its own and one on its way out is still running for a moment; it is not there to make the test easier, and the scaling was chosen after measuring the leak at one, three and five cycles and finding it exactly linear.

Each cycle also hands the running server real work and waits for it, and hands the stopped server sixteen more units afterwards, so what is counted is a server that was used and then stopped rather than one that was only started. That is what closes the other edge of the same queue: the send that delivers a task is itself a goroutine, and a tree that ends the consumer's wait and leaves that send alone parks one per late hand-over. Sixteen rather than two because a hand-over that ends because a buffer happened to have room for it has not ended for the right reason; measured, a tree with an eight-deep queue and no cancellation on the send parks 48 and fails.

The work handed over is held by the test until it has checked two more things about the service that is running it. The hand-over must have come back while that work is still running -- a tree that answers every question here by running the task on whatever goroutine submitted it leaks nothing, because it starts nothing, and is also no longer a task queue. And a second unit handed over while the first is held must not run until the first is done -- a tree that answers instead by starting a goroutine per unit of work has not given anything a lifetime either, it has just made every lifetime short. Both are stated in requirement 3 of the instruction, both are true of the two trees this step starts from, and both are therefore properties to preserve rather than to acquire.

The second test names what the first counts: starting and stopping one server adds no goroutine whose stack is inside the package that runs its tasks. A count can be argued with -- something else might have made the number -- and a stack cannot. It is a difference against a baseline taken before that server starts, so a leak an earlier test in the same process left behind is not charged to this one.

The third stops six servers at once, because shutdown that is only correct when it happens alone is not shutdown. Each of them has run work before it is stopped, for the same reason as the first.

Measured on seven trees: the reference passes all five tests; both starting trees fail exactly these three and pass both controls; a tree that runs submitted work on the submitter's own goroutine fails all three; a tree that starts a goroutine per unit of work fails all three; a tree that deletes the executor outright fails all five; and a tree that does the consumer half and leaves the producer half alone fails the count test and one control, scoring 8 of this gate's 12.

Budget: 6 m against 25 s measured. A tree that cannot start a server at all fails `serve` on the first test and costs nothing. A tree that never runs the work it is given waits out a 15 s deadline in each test instead -- measured at 68 s, still an order inside the budget -- and a tree whose Close blocks costs the whole budget, which is the case the rest of the headroom is for.

The task line's '-race under seeded stress' (migration review round 2, 2026-10-05). An earlier draft of this gate was withdrawn because toolenv sets CGO_ENABLED=0 and the race detector refuses to start without cgo; that is this verifier's own setting, the image (golang:1.25.14-bookworm) ships gcc, and the gate now sets CGO_ENABLED=1 for its two runs only. It also no longer asks the repository's own suite to go green -- only to print no race report -- which was the other reason for the withdrawal.

Two runs. The repository's own tests, `go test -race -count=1 -shuffle=20261005 ./...`, read for race reports only. And the cleanup probe package under `-race -count=3 -shuffle=20261005`: the same three graded tests as probe:cleanup, each of which must pass in all three repetitions. Score = graded tests that held in every repetition / 3, and 0 if either run printed `WARNING: DATA RACE` or had to be killed. Both are stated in requirement 6 of the instruction, seed and repetition count included.

Calibrated in this step's verifier image, uid 65534, --cpus=4: the reference solution passes 15/15 probe tests with 0 race reports (81 s) and its own suite prints 0 race reports under count=1 and count=2 with this seed (the 2017 vfs suite can still fail a spec under load; that is not read here). The untouched step-7 tree prints 0 race reports and fails the three graded tests, so it reads 0 -- a migrated gate, as rule 2 requires. A tree that fixes the leak the reference's way but ends the executor loop by polling a plain `stopped bool` that Close sets prints 5 race reports and reads 0 here while it would pass probe:cleanup's leak counts.

The package that runs a server's tasks reaches the standard library's cancellation vocabulary. Measured: no file under `api/server/services` imports `context` on either of the trees this step can start from, and the reference solution's does.

This is a statement about vocabulary rather than about implementation. A bespoke `quit chan struct{}` can stop a goroutine too, and would pass the probe; what it cannot do is compose -- it does not carry a deadline, it cannot be handed to anything that already takes a context or derived from anything that already has one, and it is not what anything else in this tree speaks after step 2 put `types.Context` through every call path. The line's subject is the modern vocabulary, and this is the one place left in the server that shuts something down without it. It carries an explicit id because step 2's own `context` import gate is inherited into this step's regression family and the two would otherwise be reported under one name. Worth 3 of 15 because it is a claim about which type is used and not about whether the leak is closed, which is the probe's job.

cancellation.why: Five tests, 3.0 s together on the finished tree and 3.0 s on the tree this step starts from; the two controls account for nearly all of it, one of them deliberately waiting two seconds for a slow answer. Every failure path in the package is a bounded select, so the budget is there for a tree that will not start a server at all rather than for one that merely fails.

deadlines.why: Four tests, and each of the two graded ones now drives its key at two values in turn rather than at one, so the package starts six servers instead of four: 56.4 s together on the finished tree and 41.2 s on the tree this step starts from, where the two graded tests fail early. Neither is the number the budget has to clear. A tree that adds a draining stop and keeps the 2017 substring sniff deadlocks every close, and this package's teardown gives up on a stop after 30 s rather than joining the deadlock -- six servers, so three minutes of teardown on top of the waiting the tests do anyway: measured at 236.6 s on that tree, with all four assertions still reported correctly. The budget is set above that so a deadlock elsewhere in the tree costs this package time and not its answers.

earlyexit.why: Four tests, every one of which is a deadline. The package's own clocks are what bound it: 3 s for a walk that has ended to have ended, asked seven times, and 5 s for a registration to complete, asked twice -- 31 s of deadline in all if every one of them runs out, which is what happens on the tree this step starts from. Measured there: 51.23 s for the four to fail, the difference being the server the service walk needs. A passing run spends none of it. Five minutes is the budget because the failure this package is built to observe is a process that has stopped making progress, and the way that shows up when it is worse than expected -- a registration queued behind a reader that is itself queued behind a writer -- is every later deadline running out in turn rather than one of them. Test order in the file is load-bearing for that reason and is documented there.

enumeration.why: Six tests in 0.08 s, measured on both of the trees this step can start from. Five of the six are in-process registrations and walks; the sixth builds a configuration with three vfs services and starts the service layer over it, which is the 0.04 s. Two minutes is for the compile, not for the tests. The one thing that can spend real time here is a producer that never ends -- these walks are all to exhaustion -- and `go test -timeout` is what ends that, below the hard timeout so the per-test dump is printed rather than killed.

errstatus.why: Six tests sharing one server, 1.07 s together on the finished tree and 1.07 s on the tree this step starts from, where the three graded tests fail on the first response they read. Neither is the number the budget has to clear. Every way this package can wait is bounded by the package itself: sixty seconds for a server that never finishes starting, fifteen for a request that is never answered, thirty for a stop that never returns. Twenty-one requests are issued in all, so the arithmetic worst case -- a server that answers every one of them just too slowly to count -- is 315 s of requests on top of a minute of start and half a minute of stop, and the budget sits above that. Bounding rather than waiting is deliberate: a tree whose server has been broken elsewhere should fail these assertions and say so, not take the package's other answers down with it.

errwrap.why: Six tests that construct errors and ask questions of them in process -- no server, no listener, no clock. 0.005 s together on the finished tree and 0.006 s on the tree this step starts from. The budget is two minutes because the only way this package can be slow is a tree that takes a long time to compile, and a compile is the one thing a test timeout should never be the first to notice.

logging.why: Eighteen tests that build a context and log to it in process -- no server, no listener, no clock -- thirteen graded bounds, the two that read the logger no context configured, and three controls that ask the same of the harness itself. 0.02 s together on the tree this step starts from: every one of them writes a handful of lines and reads them back. Two minutes for the reason the other the compile, not the tests. The one thing this package does that is not ordinary is redirect file descriptors 1 and 2 into a pipe for the duration of each call and restore them afterwards, including on the way out of a panic; the reader is drained in a goroutine so a logger that writes more than a pipe buffer cannot block, and the first of the three controls is there to fail loudly if any of that stops working.

rooted.why: Seven tests, each of which brings up one vfs service the way the server does and drives the driver behind it: 0.12 s together on the tree this step starts from, 0.16 s on the other tree it can start from, and 0.13 s on the finished tree. Nothing here waits for anything, so the budget is not for the tests -- it is for a tree whose service registry will not initialise, where every one of the seven spends its time in configuration loading before failing.

routing.why: Eight tests against one server. The package starts a single real server on a loopback port with a single vfs service in TestMain, seeds one volume through it, and every test drives raw requests at that one instance: 34 request/response pairs in all, 1.08 s together on the tree this step starts from, because the requests are loopback round trips against an in-process driver. The budget is ten minutes rather than one for the failure modes, not for the passing case. A routing table the candidate has changed fails in two shapes. The fast shape is a pattern the standard router rejects: `net/http.ServeMux.Handle` panics rather than returning an error, the panic happens in TestMain before the first test, and the binary dies in 0.099 s reporting nothing -- measured, with a deliberately malformed pattern -- which is 0/8 and costs no clock at all. The slow shape is a server that starts and then answers late or not at all, and that one is bounded by the deadlines the package carries rather than by the harness killing it: 20 s to start, 10 s to become ready, 15 s on each of the seed request and the 34 graded ones, 10 s to stop, which is 550 s if every single request runs out its deadline. Ten minutes sits above that, so `go test -timeout` never truncates the run and every assertion is reported as its own pass or fail; the 660 s hard timeout sits above the `go test` one so that the Go-side timeout is always what fires, since that prints a panic dump after the `--- PASS` lines the parser has already seen, while a hard kill would lose them. One more thing, and it is not about the budget. This package's subject carries a race that predates the migration and that no step on this ladder touches: `taskTrack` in `api/server/services/services_task.go` takes the next task id from `len(s.tasks)` under the read lock and inserts under the write lock, so two registrations that overlap claim the same id, and a request that waits for a task can be left waiting on one that nobody will complete. It is verbatim in the 2017 tree. The symptom is always the same shape -- one request of the 34 never answered, its 15 s deadline reached, one test failed -- and it was measured at 3 gradings in 44 across the archive on the weight-2 controls gate, one of those three on a reference solution, with one further sighting in 46 on the weight-10 half beside it. A gate that reads 0 on a tree that answered every question correctly, one run in fourteen, is scoring a coin toss. Asking the same request again inside the same process does not help and was measured not helping: the second attempt reaches its own deadline, because what is stuck is the server's waiter and not the client's request. A fresh process does help, which is why `retry` is set here and nowhere else. It costs one more execution of this package, and only on a tree that has already failed something in it.

schema.why: Five tests. Three of them walk the whole repository: one parses every `.go` file in it, one finds every schema document in it and asks `go/build` for the embed patterns of the directories above each one, from the document's own directory up to the repository root, and the third reads the fourteen makefiles it passes on the way. The other two parse the schema document and drive the validator. 0.103 s together on the tree this step starts from and 0.096 s on the finished one, measured five tests at a time. Seven hundredths of that is the literal walk, which is the only one that parses every `.go` file in the repository; the embed reader asks `go/build` rather than the parser and the other three are a hundredth of a second each. The budget is two minutes because the only way this package can be slow is a tree that takes a long time to compile, and a compile is the one thing a test timeout should never be the first to notice.

sequences.why: Six tests and twelve compile-time assignments, in process, against one registry and one small server. Nothing here waits on anything: the tests register a handful of values, walk them, and count. The budget is five minutes for the failure modes rather than for the passing case. The commonest failure is the fastest -- a producer whose type is wrong makes the package fail to build, which is reported in seconds and scores 0 on the gate over it -- and the slowest is the one the budget is for: a sequence whose body never returns false when `yield` does, walked by a test that stops early, does not hang here (no test in this package stops early; that is the other package's subject) but a producer that yields forever does, and `go test -timeout` is what ends it. The hard timeout sits above the Go-side one so the Go-side one always fires first: it prints a panic dump after the `--- PASS` lines the parser has already read, where a hard kill would lose them.

shutdown.why: Four tests, 40.6 s together on the finished tree and 4.2 s on the tree this step starts from, where every stop returns at once and every assertion fails the moment it is made. Neither is the number the budget has to clear. The worst measured case is the half-done tree that adds a draining stop and keeps the 2017 substring match, which deadlocks the close: there each test waits out its own ceiling and then pays a further 30 s of bounded teardown for a stop that was never going to return, 288.4 s in all, with all four failures still reported rather than lost with a killed binary. A tree that drains but sets no deadline is the other slow case, at 80.7 s. The budget sits well above the deadlocking tree because bounding the teardown exists precisely so that this package still answers on a tree whose close hangs, and a package timeout would take those answers away again.

simtime.why: Five tests. Three of them wait out real time because the subject is a lifetime measured on the wall clock -- a half-second each for the expiry and no-lifetime cases, and 2.9 s for the sliding-lifetime control, which reads an entry five times a quarter of a lifetime apart and then waits out two lifetimes; the fourth is the interleave test, which carries its own ten-second deadline so that a store which stops answering reports that instead of hanging until the package clock runs out. Measured at 13.7 s together on both of the trees this step can start from, where that deadline is spent in full, and at 3.9 s on the finished tree, where the interleave test costs 0.08 s to 0.27 s. The interleave test is deliberately built so that whether it stops is the code's decision and not the scheduler's -- a thousand entries in the store, so a view of it spends nearly all of its time between an outer acquisition and an inner one, and a writer that keeps writing until the reader is done. An earlier version with one entry and a writer that ran out of work was measured passing on one of the two starting trees and failing on the other, from identical store source; the rebuilt one was measured 7 times on each, 7 failures at 10.00 s and 7 passes. The budget is set well above the failing number so that a slow machine cannot turn a deadlock into a package timeout, which would lose the controls as well.

store.why: Ten tests that construct a `types.Store` and read values back out of it in process -- no server, no listener, no clock. 0.014 s together on the tree this step starts from. Two minutes for the same reason as the package above: the compile, not the tests.

surface.why: Two tests, each of which starts an embedded server and a client through `libstorage.New` and makes one request: 2.3 s together on the finished tree and 2.2 s on the tree this step starts from. The budget is sized for the two ways a tree can be slow here rather than wrong -- `libstorage.New` itself hanging, which the helper gives up on after 60 s, and a stop that never returns, which the teardown gives up on after 30 s. Measured against the deadlocking tree: 62.4 s, both assertions still reported.

sweeper.why: One test, in simulated time, so it costs 11 ms on a tree that passes it and 11 ms on a tree that panics out of it. The budget is large only because a tree that does not compile against this package has to be given time to say so.

regression.why: Requirement 8. Inherited and still a bound rather than a milestone, and in this milestone it is the check most likely to be the first to speak. Three of the five clauses are the kind of port where the obvious edit does not compile: `math/rand/v2` has no `NewSource`, no `Intn` and no `Read`, so `rand.New(rand.NewSource(time.Now().UnixNano()))` and the three `Intn` calls beneath it all have to be rewritten rather than re-imported; the standard router panics at registration time on a pattern it cannot parse, which is a run-time failure rather than a compile-time one and is the reason the routing probe exists as well as this gate; and `log/slog` has no `Entry` type, so every one of the thirty files that names one has to be rewritten rather than re-imported.

Requirement 8. Computed from the import graph, so a dependency copied back into the repository under any directory name and rewired with a replace directive is still third-party source here. The same requirement has a second reading, because the graph cannot see a dependency whose source has been copied *into* the main module and given a first-party import path: every first-party file is also hashed, whitespace removed, against every .go file in the module cache the image ships, and a file that matches one of them is that dependency's source under another name. This milestone retires four third-party libraries at once. Copying any of the four in under a first-party name -- a `api/types/logrus` holding the text formatter, an `api/server/mux` holding the router -- is the shape the cheapest wrong answer takes, and it is the shape this gate is looking for.

Requirement 8. `replace` would let a package be aliased back in under a name of the candidate's choosing; `ignore` would let a file that no longer compiles disappear from every `./...` pattern, including the import graph the gates above read. Note what this does *not* forbid: three of the libraries this milestone retires are reached by dependencies of this module as well as by this module, so they stay in `go.mod` as indirect requirements after the last first-party import of them is gone. The gates that read this milestone read the import graph, not the requirement list, for exactly that reason.

Requirement 8. The tree this step starts from is `gofmt -s` clean -- 0 dirty files out of 163 -- so the baseline is zero and any excursion is new. The standard router's patterns are string literals and cost this gate nothing; what does is the shape of the work, which is thirty files edited by hand in one pass, and the commonest way that ends is one import block left in the order the editor found it.

Requirement 8, and on this rung it is ground rather than a milestone check. The tree this step starts from leaves `go vet ./...` silent, so the bound is silence. The previous milestone had it under real load -- the `slog` analyser reads a structured call whose arguments do not pair up -- and this one does not: nothing `vet` reports is specific to a sequence, because a function whose signature is not one of the three range-over-func shapes is a compile error and `build-all` is what hears it. What keeps this gate interesting is the shape of the work rather than its subject. Twelve function bodies in five packages are rewritten by hand, and each of them loses a `go` statement, a `close` and a `return` at once; `unreachable` and `nilfunc` both live in the default analyser set, and a body edited down to its new form with one statement left below the new `return` is reported here and nowhere else.

Requirement 8's last clause. The check class is SA1019, deprecated identifiers, and the baseline is zero. Unlike the previous rung, where `math/rand`'s top-level `Seed` put it under load, nothing this milestone names is deprecated or near a deprecation: `iter`, `unique` and the sequence adapters in `slices` and `maps` are all additions. It is carried because a tree that reaches for an older spelling to get out of a difficulty -- and the collection clause is where that temptation lives -- is told so here.
Requirement 6: silencing a tool is not fixing what it found. Zero today, and the bound is zero. `//lint:ignore SA1019` over an `io/ioutil` import is the specific thing this forecloses.
Requirement 6. One `t.Skip` exists in the inherited corpus; a second is a test that stopped running.

Requirement 6's last clause. 97 on the tree this step starts from, and the bound does not move: nothing in this milestone trades a returned value for a discard. The two places it could have -- the path variable that was read out of a map and is now read off the request, and the level that was parsed out of a string -- both still have an error or an ok to deal with, and dealing with it is the work. What the bound forbids is the ninety-seven becoming ninety-eight: shedding one is free, acquiring one is not.

Requirement 6. 84 `Test...` functions on the tree this step starts from and none of them may go. This milestone touches no test file for a reason of its own: the logging and routing layers it rewrites are exercised by the recorded corpus and by the verifier's own probe packages, neither of which lives in the tree, so a candidate who finds a test inconvenient here has no honest reason to have opened it.
Requirement 6. Ginkgo specs, counted separately from test functions because the integration suites are written in them.

Requirement 6, and the bound does not move: 493, where it was set on the previous rung and for the reason recorded there -- `astcount` counts a logging call on a method chain as an assertion, because the clause that catches `t.Errorf` reached through a struct field cannot tell the two apart, and the previous milestone deleted eight such log statements. This milestone deletes none. Measured, rather than assumed: the twelve producer bodies, the middleware helper requirement 3 retires, the six collection loops and the eight case-folding sites in the registry hold no call to `Error`, `Errorf`, `Fatal` or `Fatalf` between them, on either of the two trees this step can start from, so the count this milestone inherits is the count it hands on -- 495 on one of those trees and 507 on the other, both well clear of the bound. What the bound forbids is the same thing it has always forbidden: buying a passing check by deleting the thing that checks.
Requirement 6.

Requirement 6 and requirement 8's last sentence. One test file is behind a build tag today (`drivers/storage/mock/tests`); a second is a suite that stopped running under a constraint rather than in the open.

Requirement 8's last sentence, and the bound that keeps the import-graph gates honest: a file tagged out of the build vanishes from `go list -deps` just as thoroughly as a file whose import was retired. 124, strict, inherited from step 5: the smallest count a tree that does everything the instructions ask can hold. This milestone neither adds nor removes a source file -- every clause of it is a rewrite in place, and the one deletion it asks for is a nine-line function, not the file it lives in. The bound is derived from what the instructions require, not from the reference's count (127), so a correct tree that added no file at steps 3 and 4 is not failed for it (wave D, 2026-10-12). Strict, for the reason step 1 recorded: proportional scoring cannot deter a single excursion against a baseline this large.

Requirement 8's last sentence, by identity rather than by count. The same twenty-one entries the previous milestones left behind, unchanged: this milestone has no reason to move any of them. Widening `//go:build darwin` or `//go:build mock` so work can be skipped, or narrowing one so it need not be done, both move this. Keys the candidate adds are not held against it, so this is a bound on loss.
Requirement 8. The `// +build` form was retired three milestones ago; a file re-acquiring one is that coming undone. Zero on both trees.

The same bound from the other side: twelve files carry a `//go:build` line and no legacy twin, on the tree this step starts from and on the finished one alike. A constraint dropped rather than kept moves this below twelve; the constraint set above says which twelve.
Requirement 7. The `golang.org/x/net/context` shim stays retired; the baseline is the four packages that reached it before it was, so the fall-off is measured on the same scale it was earned on.
Requirement 7, the same bound on the subpackage.

Requirement 7. The standard library's `context` stays live in the five first-party packages that deal in a context type. This milestone rewrites import blocks in a dozen files; a sweep that reorganised them and broke the plumbing would fail this while the two absence bounds above stayed clean.
Requirement 7. The pre-Go-1.7 twin stays gone; a file reintroduced under either name is a milestone coming undone.
Requirement 7, observed. The server's configured read and write timeouts keep taking effect at the values they are configured with.
Requirement 7, observed. Stopping the server still drains what it is serving and still closes its idle connections.

Requirement 7, observed. The drain is still bounded, so a request that never finishes still cannot keep the process alive forever. It is the half of that milestone most easily lost by accident, which is why it is carried separately here too.
Requirement 7, observed. A cancelled or expired context still stops an in-flight request promptly, and a live one still completes however long the answer takes.
Requirement 7, observed. A server on the documented defaults still does not cut off a slow client, and a server with the timeouts configured still serves an ordinary request.
Requirement 7, observed. A server with nothing to drain still stops at once.

Requirement 7, observed, and the widest of the inherited bounds: the exported surface that deals in contexts is written out as ordinary code the compiler has to agree with, and the root package's `New` is driven end to end. A generic helper introduced in the wrong place changes an exported signature, and this is what notices.
Requirement 7, observed. Fifteen error messages stay what they are and every error type the repository hands out stays recognisable as itself.

Requirement 7, observed, on the part of the error API that is least visible and cheapest to break: six marshalled shapes, field for field. Carried at the inherited price of 2 rather than at the 4 the milestone that introduced it gave it -- an inherited bound is worth what every other inherited bound is worth, and the family it sits in is half again as large as it was.
Requirement 7, observed from outside the process: the plain statuses the server produces, and both shapes an error response takes, field for field.

Requirement 7, observed. An error that answers for an outcome keeps its own answer: a partly completed batch is still a server error whatever stopped it, asked at a cause that is a 400 in its own right and at one that is a 404. The control for `probe:cleanup`. Every assertion in the migrated family is satisfied by a server that never starts anything, and by one that tears itself down so eagerly that it stops answering; this dials the listener while the server is running, hands it a unit of work and waits for that work to run, and so asks whether it is still both reachable and useful. The second control rules out the two wrong ways to end the executor's wait. Tearing the queue down rather than telling the loop to stop turns a late submission into a panic, and stopping only the consumer leaves the sender parked forever; both read as a leak or a crash here, and both trees this step can start from pass it unchanged.
